extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, in-house patent counsel, and judges evaluating §101/Alice issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for determining patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo framework), including when §101 determinations are premature and how courts weigh factual issues, claim construction, and inventive-concept analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed-to inquiry: abstract idea vs technological solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea (or other judicial exception) or to a technological solution to a technological problem (a specific device, improvement, or concrete solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts contrast claims that are 'directed to an abstract idea' with claims directed to 'a purportedly revolutionary technological solution to a technological problem' or to a 'specific device' or 'allegedly improved' technological tool. Examples: WYSIWYG webpage editor held technological solution; roof-model creation through correlating data points held not abstract; radar-alert claims held directed to improving radar detectors by reducing false alerts; videoconferencing claims held directed to a specific device/switch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept (Alice step two)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying an abstract idea or natural law, determine whether the claims contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claim into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventive concept may exist where the claim recites a specific, novel implementation or improvement over the prior art (e.g., a specific solution to a problem, nonconventional steps, or particular limitations). Conversely, absence of an inventive concept is found where claims merely recite conventional, routine, well-understood activities or only instruct to apply a natural relationship in a routine manner (examples: feedback-based message distribution lacked inventive concept).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to laws of nature or natural phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claims are 'directed to' a law of nature or natural phenomenon (which are judicial exceptions to §101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include claims that effectively cover core body temperature measurement or natural genotype–drug response relationships. Even when directed to a natural law, claims can be eligible if they incorporate inventive concepts that apply or transform the law into a patentable application (e.g., Vanda, arterial thermometer decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of treatment claims (dosage/population) supports eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment claims that recite specific dosages, administration ranges, and specific patient populations can be 'directed to' a new way of using a drug rather than to a mere natural relationship, supporting eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vanda: claims reciting specific doses for a genotype and explaining how dosage correlates with QTc risk were held directed to a method of treatment rather than merely a natural relationship. Pain-treatment and antipsychotic examples: claims that specify extended-release formulations or dosage steps for a specific patient group found eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming a natural discovery into an improved process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that take a natural discovery and employ it to create a new, improved, and useful process or technique can be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid Litigation/CellzDirect: inventors discovered cells' survival characteristics and then 'employed their natural discovery to create a new and improved way' of preserving hepatocytes, claiming more than the natural phenomenon itself; the improvement and utility supported eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical device / tangible components favor eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting a physical device or substantial tangible components are less likely to be characterized as abstract ideas and more likely to be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claims to a physical device improving prior art (wireless transceiver transmitting authorization codes over protocols), imaging hardware/process for creating breast prosthetics (alignment markers and 3D modeling), and roof-model creation via non-stereoscopic aerial views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific technical improvement / solution to prior art problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a specific technical means for overcoming a problem in the prior art are indicative of an inventive concept and support eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts cite improvements such as novel sequencing-template methods for nanopore sequencing, improved mobile handset geo-location overcoming GPS receiver limitations, base-station selection requiring new indices to avoid call interruption, and novel methods of applying multiple energies concurrently to change material properties. The specification's explanation of benefits over prior art can bolster the inventive-concept finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that merely report physiological responses or natural relationships may be ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: If claims only claim the discovery/reporting of a natural relationship or physiological response and do not add inventive application, they may be ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissenting and majority opinions highlight that merely claiming the natural law (e.g., relationship between genotype and QTc) without more than routine application can fail step two. Chief Judge Prost noted that optimization or instruction to apply a natural law in a routine manner is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity undermines inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: If claimed elements are shown to be well-understood, routine, and conventional at the time of the invention, they do not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate factual record to determine whether elements were conventional; if so, this disfavors eligibility. Example: judge dissent arguing claimed temperature-detection elements were long known and conventional. Berkhimer/Aatrix emphasize underlying factual disputes about conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea categories: organizing, collecting, analyzing, reporting, and fundamental economic practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that essentially perform abstract activities—organizing data, collecting/analyzing/reporting results, or traditional business practices—are likely to be characterized as abstract ideas unless tied to a specific technical improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: blood-sample analysis claims were characterized as 'collecting, analyzing, and reporting results' (abstract) but saved by a specific novel implementation; other data-processing claims deemed ineligible when merely organizing human behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims rooted in computer technology to solve a computer-specific problem
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim addresses a problem specific to computer networks/technology and the solution is necessarily rooted in computer technology, courts may find an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claims describing solutions to problems arising in computer networks (improved data extraction/mapping from resumes, systems that necessarily require digital implementation) have survived §101 challenges when tied to technical improvements in computing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction often required before resolving §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts frequently defer a definitive §101 ruling until after claim construction where claim meaning affects whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea or contains an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts repeatedly held that claim construction is necessary because §101 analysis can hinge on claim term meanings, representation of dependent claims by a representative claim, and factual disputes that cannot be resolved at the pleadings stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-claim use considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a representative claim to decide eligibility for a group of claims, courts consider (1) whether the non-representative claims are adequately represented, (2) whether claim construction issues must be decided first, and (3) whether any provable set of facts could render some claims eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have explained these three considerations explicitly when denying motions that relied on a single representative claim to cover many dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual disputes over inventive concept make §101 premature
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are underlying factual disputes relevant to whether a claim provides an inventive concept (e.g., whether steps were conventional), courts may find §101 resolution premature and decline to grant dismissal or summary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berkheimer and Aatrix: the district court erred by concluding no underlying factual questions exist; remands occurred when factual record was needed to assess inventive-concept issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims describing concrete technological concepts (e.g., display screen, applet) may avoid being labeled abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: When the purported abstract idea is described with concrete technological components in the specification/claims, courts may be less willing to treat the claim as an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted-advertising example: the specification incorporated a display screen and an applet—'two seemingly concrete concepts'—undermining defendant's argument that the claims were directed to an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility can depend on the claimed result vs claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts caution against focusing only on the physical result of the invention rather than the invention itself when assessing whether claims are directed to patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: breast-prosthesis imaging case noted that focusing 'only on physical or tangible results' may 'inappropriately focus on the result ... rather than the invention itself.' The analysis should consider claimed steps and how they achieve the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification-discussed benefits and nonconventionality can support inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit statements in the specification about benefits, nonconventional methods, or advantages over prior art can help demonstrate that claims contain an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: arterial thermometer claims noted 'transform[ing] the underlying natural laws into inventive methods and useful devices' with record evidence of nonobvious combination; ultrashort pulsed lasers claims relied on specification describing improved functionality for particular purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that recite novel and useful structural limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural or compositional limitations that are novel and useful (e.g., specific layered lamination) can weigh in favor of eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: tissue graft claim where amnion and chorion layers being 'directly laminated to each other' was novel and useful and supported denial of dismissal on §101 grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims improving a device's functionality as a technological tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that improve a device's operation or accuracy (making it a better technological tool) can be treated as patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: heart-rate monitor improvement, radar detector improvements by reducing false alerts, and improved methods for generating an intraoral model were treated as technological improvements supporting eligibility findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that are mere optimization of existing treatments may fail inventive-concept analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Optimization or minor adjustment of existing treatments—without non-routine application—may not supply the inventive concept required under Alice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chief Judge Prost's dissent warned that labeling an adjusted dosage as merely an 'optimization of an existing treatment' can indicate failure to meet the inventive-concept requirement if no more than routine application of a natural law is claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims framed as industrial step-by-step processes for producing tangible products
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims claiming step-by-step industrial processes that produce a tangible product (e.g., one-color glass from recycled mixed-color glass) may be considered not directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: glass recycling method was held not directed to an abstract idea because it claimed a concrete industrial process with steps to create a product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural posture and participation can render Alice determination premature
rubrics_metrics.description: If procedural circumstances (e.g., not all defendants have participated) or incomplete development of the record exist, courts may decline to decide Alice issues prematurely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A court declined to address Alice issues when not all defendants in related cases had raised the issue because a ruling would affect all defendants and the court preferred opportunity for full participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: District courts may deny §101 dismissal where differences among claims or insufficient representative analysis exist
rubrics_metrics.description: When defendants rely on a single claim as representative without adequately showing it represents all asserted claims, or where there are 'real differences among the claims,' courts may deny eligibility-based dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine whether defendants articulated why each dependent claim relates to the same abstract idea or lacks inventive concept; failure to do so can prevent dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing that claimed computer functions were not previously well-known preserves eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If defendants cannot show that the claimed computer functions were well-understood, routine, or conventional in the industry, courts may find that the claims could contain an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: denial of judgment where defendants failed to provide evidence that use of persistent mainstreams/substreams were previously known; lack of such evidence supported survival of claim.
